messages.body_plain:
I comment in line below :

I'm having trouble understanding this documentation:

censoredInt - Missing values are censored or at random. Default is Null, which assumes that all NA intensites are randomly missing. 'NA' assumes that all 'NA's in 'Intensity' column are censored. '0' uses zero intensities as censored intensity. In this case, NA intensities are missing at random.

First, little more details about new options. Detailed theory and method are preparing for the manuscript. However, it will take some time. So, here is brief idea how to use new options. ‘summaryMethod’ means linear model. ‘censoredInt’ means how to use missing values and what assumptions you have. (missing at random or censored(no value because intensity is under limit of detection))

   1) missing at random : no impute, no contribution for model

   2) censored : contributed for the model, here survival model used. (caution: MSstats will not impute any value in each missing value. they are just contributed for parameter estimation.)

     1. summaryMethod=“linear”, censoredInt=NULL : all NAs are randomly missing

     2. summaryMethod=“linear”, censoredInt=“0” : only zero is censored, NA is random missing. Therefore NAs are no contribution. however, ‘0’ will be contributed in model with assumption under limit of detection. (This option is for Skyline output. Skyline distinguish random missing(NA) and censored(0))

     3. summaryMethod=“linear”, censoredInt=“NA” : all NAs are censored. Therefore all NAs are contributed with assumption under limit of detection

     If we have any ‘censored’ assumption (such as censoredInt=“0” or “NA”), we need to assume about limit of detection(here we call ‘cutoffCensored’.

cutoffCensored=“minFeature” means limit of detection will be minimum value for each feature (Each feature has the same limit of detection). cutoffCensored=“minRun” means that limit of detection will be minimum value for each run (Each run has the same limit of detection).

Does this mean Null and 0 are equivalent if I have no zero values? That is the most confusing part.

- Yes, If you don’t have zero, you have only NAs. and here we assume that all NAs are randomly missing.

The "missing.action" parameter is no longer present, so I'm not sure what it is going to do.

Also, when it says "missing at random" does this mean that the missing values are treated as unknowns rather than being imputed or removed?

- with ’missing at random’ assumption, missing values will not be imputed, and no contribution for fitting model

- just one clarification about ’remove’ : ‘remove’ in MSstats v2 means remove features which are completely missing in a certain group (no measurement in a certain group). For example, with ‘remove’ in MSstats v2, if you have missing values, but there is at least one measurement in each group, that feature will be kept and NAs is no contributed.

We have a PRM dataset that includes what we believe are true-zero missing values (missing because the feature is not there) and also randomly missing values. We would like to include as much data as possible in our calculations, which means a) treating the true-zero values are very low intensity, and b) including features with some randomly missed values, if it improves the model.

What is the appropriate setting for this type of data?

- First, we need to clarify whether you can distinguish true-zero missing values and randomly missing values. what I’m not clear that ’true-zero missing values’ means zeros or NAs.

- if you have zeros for true-zero values and NAs for missing values, it seems similar with Skyline output. then you can do two things

     1. use summaryMethod=“linear”, censoredInt=“0”, cutoffCensored=“minFeature” or “minRun” : then ‘zero’ will be contributed with values close cutoffCensored value.

     2. impute very low intensity for zero values (zero values in ‘Intensity’ column will generate error message because zero can’t be log transformed), then use censoredInt=NULL (or “0” also generate the same result). To impute very low intensity that you want (here I use 1), use the commend below before using ‘dataProcess’

          raw[raw$Intensity==0,”Intensity”]<-1

My impression was that MSstats needed complete data (and would impute a low value).

- MSstats doesn’t need complete data. now fillIncompleteRows=TRUE in dataProcess option can handle incomplete data structure. (If I misunderstand ‘complete’ data, please let me know.) the strategy for imputing is based on your assumption. if you want different imputation strategy, please let us know. Simple imputation can be done simple commend. We also can help for this part.

It looks like this may have changed but I can't find a description of what it is doing now.

- We are preparing new user manual. As soon as we finish, we will post it. Sorry for inconvenience. However, we will try to answer the question about new options here, google group.

Hope to be helpful. Please let me know if you have any further question.

-Meena

messages.body_plain:
Dear James,

You are correct. We are retiring the option 'restricted scope of biological conclusions'. It used to be appropriate for older datasets (small sample size, large technical variation), but is no longer appropriate for the typical current experiments, and tends to overfit. We suggest that all  the analyses are now done with the option 'expanded scope of biological conclusions'

The option 'restricted scope of technical replication' is only hard-coded for label-based experiments. It leads to faster runtimes, and is more conservative than  'expanded scope of technical replication'. We therefore decided to fix it for the experiments with labeled references.

HTH
Olga

messages.subject: Re: Maxquant output converter function
messages.body_plain:
Dear Brett,

Using LFQ as input to MSstats is inappropriate.

As far as I understand, LFQ is calculated by (1) calculating a ratio of peptide intensity for all pairs of samples and all peptides that are shared between the pairs, (2) for each pair of samples, calculating the median protein ratio over the peptides, (3) take the protein ratios above for all pairs of samples as input to a system of linear equations, and estimate the individual protein abundances in each sample using least squares, and (4) rescale the resulting values to preserve the total intensity of the protein over all the samples.

As you can see, the values of LFQ are obtain by a joint analysis of all the data that pertain to this protein in the experiment. Therefore, the assumptions of MSstats (at least, these of independence) are not appropriate. Since the values of LFQ are already 'consensus' estimates obtained by least squares, the MSstats workflow on these values will underestimate the actual variability in the data and will lead to overly optimistic results.

HTH
Olga

messages.body_plain:
Dear James,

I will let Meena comment on the details of the implementation. But I can comment on the reason for retiring some options.

In the last year we had two very frequent types of user feedback:

(1) The restricted scope of conclusions is often mis-interpreted or mis-used. This is only meant for severely under-powered screening experiments with noisy data. It has more statistical power, and provides to the user some initial hits, but the hits will not be necessarily reproduced. Unfortunately the restricted scope of conclusions is often used as a way to obtain small p-values, without stating the limitations of the results. To avoid creating unrealistic expectations we decided to retire this option. This decision is similar to the analysis of gene expression microarrays. E.g., early versions of Limma allowed restricted scope of biological replication, but later case studies and examples (using better quality data) did not encourage that.

(2) The run-time of MSstats needs to be improved. In the effort to improve the run-time, we looked for changes/improvements to the model. One such change involves the handling of experiments with label-based references. In these experiments, specifying 'restricted scope of technical replication' leads to slightly more conservative results (i.e., slightly less significance - the extent depends on the between-run variation, see the supplementary materials in Chang et al for the specific details), but the run time improves. In the interest of reproducibility and run-time, we decided to retire the alternative options.

I will let Meena comment on the availability of other options in other cases. But I hope that my answer clarifies the underlying motivation.

Sincerely
Olga

2. about scope of conclusion for label-based experiment vs for label-free
     - the reason that Prof. Vitek mention that 'restricted scope of technical replication' is only hard-coded for label-based is that there is no scope of technical replicates for label-free in any MSstats version (no 'RUN' term in linear model for label-free experiment). 'restricted' or 'expanded' scope of technical replicate matter only for label-based experiment in SRMstats and MSstats v2. From v3, 'RUN' is fixed, which means restricted scope of technical replicate.
3. from v3, we have different model strategy. we are preparing the document for more details. In brief, scope of biological conclusion is 'expanded' and fixed Run (restricted scope of technical replicates) for both label-free and label-based experiment.

messages.subject_clean: Problem with data format exported from Skyline (version 3.1.0.7382 64-Bit)
messages.body_plain:
When you are exporting from Skyline, you should use the "File > Export > Report" menu item, and, on the Export Report dialog, choose "Invariant" in the Language dropdown.
If you export from the Document Grid, or if you don't choose "Invariant" for the language, then the column names will have spaces in them (e.g. "Fragment Ion")

The MSstats external tool does some processing on the data before calling the MSstats main functions.  You can see that code here:
https://svn.code.sf.net/p/proteowizard/code/trunk/pwiz/pwiz_tools/Skyline/Executables/Tools/MSstats/MSStatsGC.r

Here is some of the code which renames the "Area" and "FileName" columns:
# change column name as Intensity
colnames(raw)[colnames(raw)=="Area"]<-"Intensity"
raw$Intensity<-as.character(raw$Intensity)
raw$Intensity<-as.numeric(raw$Intensity)

# change column name 'FileName' as Run
colnames(raw)[colnames(raw)=="FileName"]<-"Run"

## impute zero to NA
#raw[!is.na <http://is.na>(raw$Intensity)&raw$Intensity==0,"Intensity"]<-NA

I am not sure whether there is any other code that you would need to run in order to transform the Skyline report into what you need for your specific purpose.

Hope this helps,
-- Nick Shulman
MacCoss Lab, University of Washington
